case_study_insert.main_stem: Serangoon Additive Works (SAW) is a cooperative in the advanced-manufacturing technology sector, operating an industrial 3D-printing bureau for marine and aerospace clients across Southeast Asia from Singapore. Founded in 2018 by Chen Wei-Lin, SAW employs a workforce of 24 and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. SAW plans to invest $480,000 in a new metal 3D-printing farm, financed by $260,000 retained profit and $220,000 from the sale of older workshop equipment. The business has fixed costs of $414,000 a year, a variable cost of $17 a unit and a selling price of $40, and currently produces 28,000 units a year. SAW faces an operational problem: machine downtime has pushed the defect rate to 6.5% and delivery delays are growing.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2026: SAW produced 7,100 parts last quarter with a defect rate of 6.5%, up from 5.1% a year ago, driving $58,000 of rework costs. Metal powder waste reached 11% of throughput. Machine uptime averaged 84% against a target of 92%. On-time delivery fell to 88%. A survey of 130 marine and aerospace buyers found 62% would pay a 15% premium for certified aerospace-grade parts and 55% require ISO 9001 certification from suppliers.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Serangoon Additive Works for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Technology Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The Monetary Authority of Singapore pushed bank lending rates up from 4.1% to 4.6%, raising credit costs for machinery finance. (2) Singapore's Employment Pass qualifying salary will rise 8.0% to $5,600 per month from July 2026, lifting wage costs for skilled foreign technicians. (3) Titanium and nickel alloy powder costs rose 15.6% year-on-year, while Singapore's marine and aerospace order books grew 7.5% over the year.

questions.question_text: SAW plans to finance its metal 3D-printing farm with $260,000 retained profit and $220,000 from the sale of older workshop equipment. Explain two advantages for SAW of using these internal sources of finance instead of a bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Internal finance costs SAW no interest and creates no repayment obligation, which protects cash at a time when rework is already draining $58,000 a quarter and the defect rate has climbed to 6.5%. A bank loan would add fixed monthly repayments on top of $414,000 annual fixed costs and could force SAW to accept restrictive conditions or collateral demands on the new metal printers — especially while lending rates have moved to 4.6%. Retained profit is the money SAW's members have already earned and chosen to reinvest.

Point 2: Selling older workshop equipment converts idle assets into $220,000 of productive capacity and frees floor space for the metal farm, without diluting cooperative member control or involving any external lender in SAW's democratic decision-making. It is faster than a loan application and approval, avoids security over the new machines, and signals fiscal discipline to the 55% of buyers who require ISO 9001-style assurance that SAW is financially stable — strengthening credibility when bidding for certified aerospace work where 62% of buyers would pay a 15% premium.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Serangoon Additive Works and its financing decision.

questions.question_text: SAW is launching certified aerospace-grade 3D-printed parts. Consider direct email marketing to procurement managers, exhibiting at aerospace trade shows, or LinkedIn case-study marketing. Which should SAW choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Direct email marketing: Email reaches procurement and quality managers at target firms cheaply, lists can be segmented by sector (marine versus aerospace), and response is measurable. However, open rates in technical industrial sales are low, compliance and consent rules apply, and procurement teams are sceptical of unsolicited claims — especially for safety-critical parts where ISO 9001 certification and atom-level material traceability matter. Email rarely closes a certified-supplier qualification alone.

Aerospace trade shows: Exhibitions let SAW demonstrate metal-printed parts, present material certificates and ISO 9001 documentation face-to-face, meet supplier-quality auditors directly, and gather live requirements. The 130-buyer survey shows 62% would pay a 15% premium and 55% demand certification — both need tangible proof that a booth interaction delivers. Drawbacks: stand, travel and staffing costs from Singapore to regional shows are high for a 24-person co-op, reach is episodic, and SAW must convert fast before the 7.5% order-book growth is captured by rivals.

LinkedIn case-study marketing: Publishing case studies — for example, a bracket that replaced a 6-week forged component with a 9-day printed one at 6.5% defect (improving) — builds authority among engineers and buyers at near-zero cost, compounds over months, and reinforces SAW's cooperative, sustainability-friendly story. Drawback is slow build-up and the risk that content is ignored without paid amplification or a strong follower base.

Recommendation: SAW should choose exhibiting at aerospace trade shows as its primary channel. Certified aerospace work is bought on trust and audited evidence, which only face-to-face demonstration and documentation review can establish quickly — precisely what 62% premium-payers and 55% certification-demanders need to see. Email is rejected as too low-trust for qualification decisions; LinkedIn is rejected as a sole channel because its slow compounding would miss the current 7.5% regional order-book window, though SAW should run LinkedIn in parallel to nurture leads between shows.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of SAW with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of SAW with a well-justified recommendation explaining why email and LinkedIn-only approaches are rejected.

questions.question_text: SAW is a cooperative using democratic leadership within a hierarchical structure. Explain two benefits for SAW of involving member-elected leads in decisions about the new metal 3D-printing farm.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic involvement gives the 24 member-owners genuine influence over machine selection, shift patterns and maintenance routines, satisfying intrinsic motivation (autonomy, mastery, purpose) and increasing commitment to the farm's success. Members who help design the metal-print process are more vigilant about powder handling and set-up verification — exactly the disciplines that cut the defect rate from 6.5% back toward the 5.1% seen a year ago and lift the 84% average uptime toward the 92% target, reducing the $58,000 quarterly rework bill.

Point 2: Hierarchical reporting through member-elected leads keeps accountability clear — each lead owns a workstream (machines, QA, delivery) and reports to the cooperative board — so democratic voice does not mean slow or chaotic decision-making. Fast escalation of downtime events protects on-time delivery (currently 88%) and client trust on certified contracts. Democratic practice also strengthens retention of skilled technicians facing the 8.0% Employment Pass salary rise, since voice and influence are non-cash rewards a cooperative can offer that cash-strapped rivals cannot easily match.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to SAW's cooperative structure, quality and retention.

questions.question_text: SAW must decide how to organise production on the new metal 3D-printing farm. Consider batch production or job production. Which should SAW choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Batch production: Printing standardised aerospace and marine parts in batches — for example 50 identical brackets per client drawing — spreads set-up time, machine calibration and powder qualification across many units, driving unit cost down toward $17 and protecting the 55.0% gross profit. It suits 28,000 units a year with 88% on-time delivery ambitions, supports JIT-style material flow, and makes QA sampling (one part per batch) statistically meaningful, catching drift before a batch is scrapped. Drawbacks: batch sizes must be forecast; over-production ties up cash and powder storage; a single contaminated batch can quarantine hundreds of parts; and batch economics discourage the tiny, one-off certified jobs some aerospace clients request.

Job production: One-off, client-specific parts — custom tooling, replacement ribs, prototype certification articles — command premium pricing (the 15% premium 62% of buyers will pay, potentially $46 per unit) and deepen client relationships. Work is varied and members' craft skills stay sharp. Drawbacks: no economies of scale, price per unit far higher than $40, slower throughput, harder QA planning, powder qualification per job, and to hit 28,000 units a year the bureau would need implausibly high volumes of small jobs; margins would erode against the $414,000 fixed-cost base.

Decision: SAW should choose batch production as the backbone of the metal farm, reserving job production as a premium service for prototype and certification work. Batch volume of standard certified parts exploits the 7.5% regional order-book growth, pushes utilisation toward the 92% uptime target and funds the fixed-cost base; pure job production is rejected because it cannot reach 28,000 units economically or defend a 18,000-unit break-even against rising powder costs. A blended job-batch hybrid — batch the certified standards, job the one-offs at premium prices — gives SAW the volume profit of batch work and the margin upside of job work, which suits cooperative members' varied skills.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two production methods with limited application to SAW.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both production methods in the context of SAW.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both production methods in the context of SAW with a well-justified decision covering cost, quality, volume and client fit.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how SAW's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $414,000 ÷ ($40 − $17) = $414,000 ÷ $23 = 18,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 18,000 units a year.

sub_parts.question_text: Calculate SAW's average total cost at the current output level.
sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Average total cost = (Fixed costs + Variable cost per unit × Output) ÷ Output. Substitution: ($414,000 + $17 × 28,000) ÷ 28,000 = ($414,000 + $476,000) ÷ 28,000 = $890,000 ÷ 28,000 = $31.79. Answer: average total cost is $31.79 per unit.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways SAW's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. SAW's managers can compare the 18,000-unit break-even with the 28,000 units produced to confirm a margin of safety of 10,000 units, giving confidence that the metal farm can absorb an early-life defect spike above the current 6.5% without slipping into loss while the certification process beds in.
2. Contribution per unit of $23 against the $40 standard price, and versus $46 for the 15%-premium certified parts preferred by 62% of surveyed buyers, lets managers decide which jobs to route to the new printers first and quantify the extra $3 per unit the certification is worth.
3. Fixed costs of $414,000 against contribution of $23 per unit stress-test the $480,000 investment financed internally, showing members at the AGM that the farm needs only a 20% volume uplift to cover its own financing, strengthening the case against taking an external bank loan at 4.6%.
4. Unit cost data — $31.79 total versus $17 pure variable cost — lets managers attack the $58,000 quarterly rework bill and 11% powder waste directly: cutting rework by a third would save about $19,000 a quarter, worth roughly $0.68 per unit across 28,000 units, compelling evidence for tightening set-up verification and powder storage discipline.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 18,000 units | (ii) Average total cost = $31.79 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 28,000-unit output; certification premium modelling on $23 contribution; internal-finance stress test for the $480,000 farm; and unit-cost benchmarking at $31.79 to attack the $58,000 rework problem.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate SAW's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Which year shows stronger performance, and has SAW's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 50.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 55.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 25.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 30.0%
ROCE 2024 = 12.5%
ROCE 2025 = 18.1%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit = $800,000 − $400,000 = $400,000; 2025 gross profit = $1,120,000 − $504,000 = $616,000. 2024 operating profit $200,000; 2025 operating profit $336,000. Returns on capital employed 2024 = $200,000 ÷ $1,600,000 = 12.5%; 2025 = $336,000 ÷ $1,860,000 = 18.1%. Operating profit expressed as a share of revenue 2025 = $336,000 ÷ $1,120,000 = 30.0%; 2024 = $200,000 ÷ $800,000 = 25.0%. Capital employed grew only $260,000 — exactly the retained-profit element of the expansion, since the remaining $220,000 came from selling older equipment (an asset swap, not new capital).

Evaluation: Performance improved decisively across all three measures. The share of revenue retained as gross profit rose from 50.0% to 55.0% as certified aerospace work lifted the price mix, and operating profit grew 68% to $336,000 despite alloy powder inflation of 15.6% — evidence members priced the premium work correctly. Returns on capital jumped from 12.5% to 18.1%, impressive given 2024's modest base and the fact the expansion was debt-free; interest payable actually fell from $30,000 to $22,000, so no funder absorbed the gain. Caveats: the 6.5% defect rate and $58,000 rework are still evidence of operational slippage, on-time delivery fell to 88%, and 2025 benefited from lumpy project recognition — 2026 must show repeatability. Risks ahead: further powder inflation, Employment Pass salary rise to $5,600, and qualification costs for ISO 9001.

Conclusion: SAW's financial performance has clearly improved. Gross profitability (50.0% to 55.0%), operating profitability (25.0% to 30.0%) and returns on capital (12.5% to 18.1%) all rose, while interest fell, giving members a stronger, cleaner balance sheet to enter the metal-printing phase. The co-op enters the expansion from strength — provided QA discipline restores uptime toward 92% and rework toward 5.1% defect levels, these gains should hold.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, costs and capital employed movements and a justified conclusion on whether SAW's financial performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for SAW of switching the new metal farm to certified aerospace-grade recycled titanium powder.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Certified recycled titanium powder unlocks the exact segment the market research points to — 62% of the 130 marine and aerospace buyers surveyed would pay a 15% premium for certified aerospace-grade parts, and 55% require ISO 9001 supplier certification. Recycled powder also cuts embodied carbon per part, a genuine differentiator in defence and sustainability-sensitive tenders, and typically costs less than virgin powder once scaled, partially offsetting the 15.6% year-on-year alloy inflation already hitting SAW's $17 variable cost. Qualification data from previous runs should shorten the certification timeline on the new farm.

Disadvantage: Recycled powder varies more in particle size and chemistry than virgin stock, and any batch drift directly feeds the 6.5% defect rate and the $58,000 quarterly rework bill — a single failed build on a $40 part erases its margin. Certification and batch testing add cost and lead time (powder must be quarantined, sampled and logged), supply of certified recycled powder is thin in Southeast Asia, and if SAW certifies against one feedstock then must re-qualify whenever the supplier changes blend, creating a recurring compliance burden that 24 members and the current 84% uptime cannot easily absorb alongside the metal-farm ramp-up.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to SAW's quality, certification and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the 4.6% lending rate, the 8.0% rise in the Employment Pass qualifying salary to $5,600 and the 15.6% rise in alloy powder costs will affect SAW. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Lending rate rise from 4.1% to 4.6%: SAW financed the metal farm internally ($260,000 retained profit plus $220,000 from selling older equipment) with no new bank borrowing, so the direct interest effect is close to zero. Indirectly, higher rates raise the cost of any future machinery finance, compress clients' capital budgets (marine yards delaying refits), and cool 7.5% order-book growth if financing dries up across the region. Because SAW is deliberately debt-light, it is better insulated than leveraged rivals — a real competitive edge that should be preserved rather than spent. Notably it also makes the cooperative's no-external-finance choice look wise in hindsight.

Employment Pass qualifying salary rise of 8.0% to $5,600 per month: SAW hires whichever skilled technicians it cannot source locally — perhaps 6 of its 24 staff — so the extra $448 per month each is about $32,300 a year of additional wage cost, roughly $2.80 per employee per month of margin across the team. Morale and fairness issues arise if local members' wages are not reviewed in step, and the tighter qualifying salary may squeeze mid-tier technicians out of Singapore entirely, worsening the skills pool for the metal farm. Mitigation: multi-skilling locals, retention bonuses below the EP threshold effect, and automation of powder handling.

Alloy powder inflation of 15.6%: This is a direct, recurring hit on the dominant input in SAW's $17 variable cost — titanium and nickel feeds for certified parts. If powder is two-thirds of variable cost (~$11.30), a 15.6% rise adds about $1.76 per unit; across 28,000 units that is roughly $49,300 a year, or 4.4% of revenue, before any recovery through price. It also raises the stakes of the 6.5% defect rate — every scrapped batch wastes more expensive powder — and of the 11% throughput waste. Locking 12-month supply contracts, qualifying a second powder source and pursuing the certified 15% premium tier all recover part of this, but nothing fully offsets it.

Conclusion: The 15.6% rise in titanium and nickel alloy powder costs will have the greatest impact. It recurs on every unit SAW produces, compounds with rework and waste at the new farm, and cannot be hedged away like debt costs. The EP salary rise is second — material (~$32,300 a year) but targetable through contracts and multi-skilling — while the 4.6% lending rate is smallest because SAW deliberately expanded without new debt. SAW should lock powder pricing, accelerate certification to defend the 15% premium, and keep its debt-light discipline.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to SAW.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on SAW's costs, demand or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of SAW with a well-justified judgment that alloy cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
